fieldsRead.text: Applied Mathematics at TU Delft combines rigorous mathematical reasoning with modelling, computation and applications. Students study analysis, algebra, probability, optimisation and numerical methods, develop models in a project sequence and complete a bachelor project.

One UCR programme combines mathematical methods with algorithms, statistics, learning systems and quantitative economic applications. It offers a related applied route, with less specialist analysis, abstract algebra and modelling-project depth than Delft.

This Dutch-taught, full-time pathway selects four mathematical electives and one non-mathematical elective. The 30-EC minor remains genuine choice space, subject to programme approval and non-overlap rules.
One 5-EC requirement consisting of 3 EC proof theory and a 2-EC practical; counted once.
Required 15-EC bachelor project after all first-year courses and at least 40 major EC from years two and three. Topic-specific essential foundations can also be required.
A coherent 30-EC minor at academic level, reaching third-year level. Individual or external packages require the applicable approval and must not overlap the major.

Partial correspondence in formal proof construction: direct and indirect arguments, quantified reasoning and induction. UCR combines proof with logic and discrete structures rather than a separate theory-and-practical pair.
Both directly teach calculus techniques used in scientific and engineering applications.
Both directly teach vectors, matrices and linear transformations; the second external linear-algebra course remains additional depth.
Partial correspondence in differential equations within UCR multivariable calculus; the Delft component concentrates on ordinary differential equations.
Both directly study numerical solution methods; UCR includes numerical differentiation, integration and ordinary differential equations.
Calculus techniques and applications are included, but no separate course centred on proof-based analysis is selected.
UCR lacks a second separately credited analysis course.
The selected Linear Algebra course occupies its stronger foundational counterpart row. There is no second separate linear-algebra course in this programme.
Advanced Calculus focuses on calculus methods and applications rather than a separate proof-based real-analysis course.
UCR studies complex-valued functions within broader calculus; no selected course centres on complex analysis and analytic-function theory.
No selected course centres on partial differential equations; broader calculus and numerical methods provide related techniques.
UCR Probability and Statistics does not reproduce measure-theoretic probability.
Algebraic algorithms address mathematical computation, while Delft has a separate course centred on abstract algebraic structures.
UCR proof, logic and discrete foundations occupy the proof-techniques row. No additional separate course is allocated to the breadth of this discrete-mathematics component.

Partial correspondence in statistical estimation, inference and tests. UCR combines statistics with empirical research design; the Delft component sits within a mathematical probability-and-statistics sequence.
Both directly cover probability distributions; UCR integrates mathematical statistics and simulation.

Partial correspondence in advanced statistical modelling through regression, multivariable models and diagnostics. UCR applies these to health and behavioural data rather than following the same mathematical elective.
Both directly teach machine-learning models and prediction; their disciplinary framing and depth differ.
Both introduce programming for computational problem solving.
Both directly concern algorithm design; UCR also treats data structures and experimental performance.

Partial graph-method correspondence through networks, maximum-flow algorithms and network science. UCR places these within algebraic algorithms and optimisation rather than a dedicated graph-theory course.
Both directly formulate and solve optimisation problems; UCR emphasises search and computational implementation.

Partial correspondence in discrete-time stochastic state models and Markov-based decisions. UCR emphasises probabilistic inference and agent policies, rather than the full discrete- and continuous-time Markov-process course.

Delft Applied Mathematics includes a cumulative proof-intensive sequence in analysis, measure-theoretic probability, abstract algebra, partial differential equations and mathematical modelling. The UCR programme combines mathematical methods with computation, statistics and quantitative applications; it does not reproduce that specialist mathematics sequence.

Develop calculus, linear algebra, probability and numerical methods through optimisation, algorithms, statistical learning and models of technical and societal systems. This is a broad applied quantitative response; it does not reproduce Delft's proof-intensive specialist mathematics sequence.
